body.text: Victorian premier Ben Carroll on the way out after a difficult four months as Labor leader
He was the premier for 123 days.
It was by no means the shortest time in leadership for a Victorian premier. It was also not the easiest.
Labor had plunged in the polls after 12 years in government and Ben Carroll walked in the shadow of two controversial leaders.

Daniel Andrews ordered one of the world's longest COVID lockdowns and kicked off Victoria's Big Build infrastructure boom, which was also under the remit of Jacinta Allan when she was public transport infrastructure minister then premier.
The project is now the subject of a royal commission into alleged crime and corruption on building sites, which was called by Mr Carroll after he took the leadership from Ms Allan.
While Mr Carroll promised a new direction for Labor, Victorians tonight decided they wanted a fresh start — including in his own seat of Niddrie.
"We are part of the longest serving Labor government in Victoria's history," Mr Carroll said during his concession speech on election night.
"We ran a strong campaign, but you can't outrun time."
Deputy Labor leader Gabrielle Williams said Mr Carroll's exit was a "huge loss" for the party and that he was "one of the most decent human beings" she had encountered in politics.
From working class to political class
Ben Carroll was born into a working class family in the northern Melbourne suburb of Airport West in 1975.
His mother was a school teacher and his father was an electrician.
Mr Carroll often spoke of growing up under the flight path, getting an after-school job at Kmart at the age of 14 and watching his father run a small business.
He studied law at university and later spent time as a volunteer lawyer at a community legal service.
He landed a job as a political advisor in 1999 to then-Labor premier Steve Bracks.
"In those early years, I had the honour of working in his office and saw up close how he brought people together as we travelled right across the state," Mr Carroll wrote in a social media post.
Mr Carroll crossed over to parliament after standing for pre-selection for the seat of Niddrie in 2012 against future cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes.
He then won the seat in a by-election after the resignation of Rob Hulls.
He started his maiden speech to state parliament by telling the story of his ancestor Michael Carroll leaving Ireland in 1840 during the potato famine and arriving on a boat in Australia.

"The reason I tell this story is to illustrate the power of opportunity: that a descendant of a labourer from Tipperary, Ireland, can now stand before you in this special place, this great chamber of history and achievement, due to the opportunity provided by a young nation to a young Irishman more than 170 years ago," he said in April 2012.

During more than 5,300 days in parliament, Mr Carroll has held 16 portfolios in a range of areas, from two stints as the minister for medical research to WorkSafe and the Transport Accident Commission, manufacturing and crime prevention.

He was the minister for education when Victorian state school teachers held their first mass strikes in 13 years and during years of blunders with VCE exams, including the leaking of exam questions, typos and errors in exams and some students being given the wrong paper.
Mr Carroll was elevated to the position of deputy premier when Dan Andrews quit as premier in 2023, handing the leadership over to Ms Allan.
In July, as Labor's popularity nosedived in the months before the state election, rumblings of a leadership challenge grew.
After assuring he was standing by Ms Allan as leader, Mr Carroll announced he would nominate for the position.
He said the change of heart came after he was visited by a delegation of Labor MPs.
"It is clear that the premier has lost the majority of our caucus," he said.
"As such, I have visited the premier to inform her that I will be nominating for the leadership of the Labor Party."
In the end, he did not have to challenge Ms Allan.
Ms Allan announced she was not only stepping down as premier but would quit politics at the state election.

However, Mr Carroll still had to face a Labor caucus meeting, which descended into chaos and yelling when Allan loyalist Sonya Kilkenny made a surprise run for the leadership — with Ms Allan adding her signature to the nomination.
In the end, Ms Kilkenny pulled out of the race to avoid a leadership battle that could have lasted weeks due to Labor's requirement that it be put to a full vote of party members.
Mr Carroll was sworn in as Victoria's 50th premier, with his first move being to call the royal commission into the Big Build.
"I am honoured and humbled to be elected unanimously as the new leader of the Victorian Labor Party," he told his first press conference as the state's leader.
"This was not an easy decision, but the stakes at this election are too high."
He also used his first day in office to telephone Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush to discuss crime and community safety.
Mr Carroll also had another big statement to make that day in his first press conference as premier.
"Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan."

In his short time in the job, he cut the number of ministers in cabinet, promised Victoria would meet its school funding obligations under the former Gonski plan and announced $2 billion worth of cuts to the Suburban Rail Loop.
Mr Carroll has described himself as relatable and hard-working.
His list of priorities on his official parliamentary biography are heavily focused on education.

He also stated that he wanted Victoria to become a world leader in mental health support and to take strong action on climate change, with a vision for the state to become a global leader in the creation of a zero-emissions, renewable workforce.
A week before the election, Mr Carroll told the ABC's state political reporter Richard Willingham he was feeling positive.
"Victoria is the best state in the greatest nation on earth," he said.
